power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .071", "p = .064"), Sentence = c("Social support theory grief severity (t = 2, p = .071), loneliness (t = 2.45, p = .033), perceived stress (t = 2.06, p = .064), and global sleep (t = 2.07, p = Six studies reported acceptability data, evidenced by posiFve and negaFve parFcipant feedback.", "Social support theory grief severity (t = 2, p = .071), loneliness (t = 2.45, p = .033), perceived stress (t = 2.06, p = .064), and global sleep (t = 2.07, p = Six studies reported acceptability data, evidenced by posiFve and negaFve parFcipant feedback." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Background: Virtual Reality (VR) might support grieving processes through therapeuFc environments that encourage conFnuing bonds with deceased loved ones.
In contrast, VR might encourage avoidance of reality among bereaved individuals and interfere with their grieving processes.

ObjecFve: This systemaFc review of studies with mixed methodological designs (i.e., qualitaFve, quanFtaFve, mixed methods) examines the acceptability, feasibility and efficacy of Virtual Reality (VR) for bereaved individuals.

Methods: A systemaFc search idenFfied studies published unFl May 2025 using terms related to grief, VR and other immersive technologies (i.e., augmented reality, mixed reality) from 4 databases (OVID Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Scopus).
Studies reporFng the use of VR or other immersive technologies for grief were included.
IntervenFon elements, efficacy outcomes, acceptability and feasibility were extracted.
Results: Out of 5'704 screened Ftles and abstracts, 9 studies met eligibility.
Types of loss included parental loss (k=1), paFent loss (k=1), loss of a spouse (k=1), gestaFonal loss (k=1), child loss (k=1), loss of a significant person (k=1), and loss of a person (k=3).
Seven studies used a webbased VR intervenFon, and two studies used a non-web-based VR intervenFon.
VR intervenFon tools included Second Life (k=2), EMMA's WORLD (k=5), AViR (k=1) and 3MDR-TG (k=1).

Our findings show modest support for preliminary VR efficacy, with three studies showing similar significant changes compared to control groups and five studies showing reducFons in grief and related distress outcomes.
VR was further shown to be feasible and acceptable for bereaved people.
Conclusions: VR research for bereaved individuals is sFll underdeveloped.

Future research should aim to determine VR efficacy and idenFfy moderaFng factors for bereaved individuals by using larger sample sizes randomized to different levels of immersion and validated grief scales to report grief symptoms.
• This systemaFc review examined the acceptability, feasibility and efficacy of Virtual Reality (VR) for bereaved individuals.
• Our findings showed VR to be feasible and acceptable among bereaved individuals, with modest support for preliminary VR efficacy.
• Future research are encouraged to use larger sample sizes randomized to different levels of immersion and validated grief scales to determine VR efficacy.
The loss of a loved one is a universally painful and inevitable experience in an individual's lifeFme.
While some individuals process grief in a normaFve manner, around 13% of people experience grief atypically (Comtesse et al., 2024).

text.text: Prolonged Grief Disorder (PGD), formerly known as complicated grief, is a separate diagnosFc category in the DSM-5-TR (2022) and the ICD-11 (2018) that captures atypical grief.

Along the core symptoms of longing for and preoccupaFon with the deceased, PGD is characterized by addiFonal symptoms such as emoFonal distress, funcFonal impairment to a clinically significant degree (6-12 months following the loss of a loved one) and a duraFon and severity of the grief response that is markedly greater than social, cultural, or religious norms for the bereaved person's culture and context (Killikelly & Maercker, 2017; Prigerson et al., 2009).

text.text: A potenFal benefit of using VR lies in its ability to provide comfort to bereaved individuals and facilitate their grieving processes through therapeuFc environments or through conFnuing bonds with their deceased loved ones (Klass et al., 2014).

text.text: A review about VR for grief is needed to get an understanding of current evidence for future research and clinical pracFce.
This systemaFc review aims to give an overview of exisFng literature that examined the efficacy, acceptance, or feasibility of virtual reality for grief.

We defined Virtual Reality as a technology that generates interacFve virtual environment designed to simulate a real-life experience, which can be divided in two categories: Nonimmersive VR which uses technology that displays the content via computer screen without addiFonal equipment, and immersive VR which uses head-mounted displays to track moFon and provide deeper immersion (Lee et al., 2013; Suh & Prophet, 2018; Wojciechowski & Cellary, 2013).

text.text: This review follows Preferred ReporFng Items for SystemaFc Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251168988).
No insFtuFonal review board approval was needed, as this study is a systemaFc review.

A literature search was conducted in May 2025 and included studies from incepFon to May 2025 reporFng on efficacy, acceptability, and feasibility of VR and other immersive technologies for bereaved people.

Included studies 1) intervened on grief, 2) implemented VR (immersive or non-immersive) or other immersive technologies (e.g., augmented reality, mixed reality), and 3) provided efficacy (i.e., grief outcomes), acceptability (i.e., parFcipant's experience) and/or feasibility (i.e., compliance and retenFon of parFcipant) outcomes.
Excluded were conference papers, protocols, reviews and video games.
An updated search was done in April 2026 and included studies from June 2025 to April 2026.
We searched OVID Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Scopus with search strings for grief and immersive technologies.
The search strings were developed with a librarian (Appendix A).
Two authors (P.G. and A.L.) screened the Ftles and abstracts for relevance.

text.text: This systemaFc review examined eight studies that used VR for bereaved individuals.

Across varying study design, grief outcomes, types of loss, and parFcipants, findings indicated high retenFon and compliance, high parFcipant liking and acceptability, as well as modest evidence of efficacy.
Future invesFgaFons are essenFal to address gaps in this literature.
Feasibility findings were scarce but indicated high compliance and retenFon rates across studies.
This is contrary to a review that reported relaFvely large drop-out rates for studies that used VR for various mental health problems, including PTSD (Valmaggia et al., 2016).

This is a finding that was not reflected in our studies, which might explain the high compliance found in our review.
Regarding acceptability, negaFve feedback was scarce and primarily related to technical problems.
ParFcipants showed high expectaFon and saFsfacFon for VR and expressed that VR intervenFons are saFsfactory and helpful in understanding their grief.

This is in line with current literature that reported high user saFsfacFon of VR intervenFons for various psychiatric disorders (Botella et al., 2015; Humbert et al., 2023; Rus-Calafell et al., 2018).

text.text: Findings regarding grief outcomes reflect a gap in the literature for VR research, with a small number of RCTs and small sample sizes limiFng a solid evaluaFon of VR efficacy or effecFveness.

These findings are consistent with a meta-review or meta-analyses with VR studies for psychiatric disorders (Dellazizzo et al., 2020), which have reported that the quality of evidence varied from very low to moderate due to a limited number of RCTs, lack of follow-up analysis or control group, heterogeneity and publicaFon bias.

text.text: EvaluaFng the overall efficacy and effecFveness of VR for grief requires more RCTs that examine specific grief outcomes with validated grief scales (e.g.
IPGDS) using a between-subjects design that compares the VR condiFon to an evidence-based and digital control condiFon.
AddiFonally, micro-randomized trials that examine the effecFveness and efficacy of specific VR features within-subject (i.e. comparing a fully immersive versus a non-immersive VR tool) are essenFal.
Although this review is sFll in an early-stage and exploratory phase, a few results warrant menFon.
First, VR intervenFons seem to show similar improvements in directly measured grief symptoms as the control condiFons.
Similarly, Dellazizzo et al. (2020) reported that VR intervenFons showed no superiority compared to evidence-based treatments.

text.text: At 12-month follow-up, we reported one study that has found a higher percentage of recovered in the VR condiFon versus the control condiFon.
This is in line with Dellazizzo et al. (2020) who reported that effects of VR intervenFons likely sustain over Fme.

text.text: The scarcity of papers, heterogeneity of study designs as well as the quality of reviewed studies preclude more firm conclusions about VR for bereaved individuals.
The reviewed papers were a mix of qualitaFve studies and small-scale trials primarily conducted in Spain, with some papers having a mixed sample (i.e. grief, PTSD, AD).
This restricts generalizability to bereaved individuals and bereaved individuals outside of Spain.
Other limitaFons further highlight areas for future research.
First, although our inclusion criteria spanned VR and other immersive technologies (i.e., augmented reality, mixed reality), all studies used VR tools, with most of them being non-immersive.
Future research should target immersive VR tools (e.g., HMD) and other immersive technologies as different levels of immersion and technologies might influence intervenFon outcomes.
Second, most studies did not report follow-up periods, which may prevent long-term efficacy outcomes to be captured.

As one study reported higher percentage of recovered in the VR condiFon versus the control condiFon in their follow-up, future research should further examine the influence of VR on efficacy outcomes compared to control condiFons.
Third, some studies did not explicitly measure grief symptoms, instead assessed individuals' general well-being with a direct measure (e.g.
PANAS) or indirect measure (e.g. narraFve well-being), which further restricted generalizability for grief outcomes.
Future research on the efficacy of VR for grief outcomes should prioriFze the use of validated grief measures.
Conclusion VR is a feasible and acceptable therapy approach for bereaved individuals, although literature about VR for bereaved individuals is scarce.

Future research with larger sample sizes, randomized trials, immersive VR tools or other immersive technologies (i.e., augmented reality, mixed reality) should aim to determine efficacy for reducing grief symptoms and idenFfy moderaFng factors influencing the efficacy.
